trails.bestSeason: Apr-Oct (icy and partly closed in winter)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, the granite steps above the Vernal Fall footbridge typically close each winter due to ice, with the John Muir Trail serving as the alternate route — expect heavy spray and slick stone even in season, especially during peak spring runoff.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail's granite steps are famously wet enough that hikers can feel the waterfall's mist from a hundred yards away during peak spring flow.

trails.bestSeason: Late May-mid Oct (cables season, weather dependent)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS and Recreation.gov, a permit is required to pass the base of the sub-dome to the cables — apply in the preseason lottery (March 1-31, results mid-April) or the daily lottery (opens two days before each hike date); the cables are scheduled to be up May 25-Oct 16, 2026, and are never safe to climb when down.
trails.didYouKnow: The final 400 feet up the cable route climbs granite pitched at roughly 45 degrees, steep enough that hikers pull themselves up hand-over-hand.

trails.bestSeason: Apr-Jun for peak flow (often dry by late summer/fall)
trails.trailTip: Flow peaks with snowmelt in May and June and the fall can slow to a trickle or run dry by late summer — visit in spring for the full roar and mist.
trails.didYouKnow: Lower Yosemite Fall is the last of three drops in the Yosemite Falls system, which together plunge 2,425 feet, one of the tallest waterfalls in North America.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, Glacier Point Road — the trailhead access — closes to vehicles each winter, typically from around November through late May depending on snowpack, so check current road status before planning a trip.
trails.didYouKnow: The dome's famous lone Jeffrey pine, made iconic by Ansel Adams photographs, died in the 1970s but its bleached snag stood for decades afterward.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, this trail shares the same Glacier Point Road access that closes each winter (roughly November through late May depending on snowpack) — the fissures at the point itself have no guardrails, so keep children close.
trails.didYouKnow: The deep vertical fissures at Taft Point drop straight to the valley floor nearly 3,500 feet below.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, the Four Mile Trail is typically closed in winter (roughly December through April) due to snow and ice on its steep switchbacks.
trails.didYouKnow: Despite the name, the trail is actually closer to 4.8 miles one-way, a naming holdover from an older, more direct alignment.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, Tioga Road — the only access to this trailhead — closes to vehicles each year with the first significant snowfall, typically by November, and often doesn't reopen until late May or June.
trails.didYouKnow: Lower Cathedral Lake sits directly beneath Cathedral Peak, the granite spire John Muir made the first recorded ascent of in 1869.

trails.bestSeason: Apr-Jun for the reflecting lake (often a dry meadow by late summer)
trails.trailTip: Visit in late spring for the classic Half Dome reflection — by late summer the lake is usually reduced to a sandy meadow as Tenaya Creek's flow drops.
trails.didYouKnow: Mirror Lake is technically a naturally forming, slowly filling pool on Tenaya Creek rather than a permanent lake, and it has been quietly shrinking for decades.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, this trailhead is reached off Tioga Road, which closes to vehicles for winter (typically November through late May/June depending on snowpack) — plan the hike for the open season.
trails.didYouKnow: North Dome offers one of the only eye-level, face-to-face views of Half Dome's sheer northwest face rather than looking up at it from the valley.

animals.viewingTip: View from at least 50 yards with binoculars and never feed a bear — Yosemite has strict food-storage rules precisely because a fed bear often has to be relocated or, in repeat cases, euthanized.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite the name, Yosemite's black bears range in color from black to blond, and the park has had no resident grizzlies since the early 1900s.

animals.whereToLook: Valley meadows near Cook's Meadow and El Capitan Meadow
animals.viewingTip: Give bucks extra space during the fall rut and never approach a fawn left alone in tall grass in late spring — the doe is usually nearby and hidden fawns are normal, not abandoned.
animals.didYouKnow: Yosemite Valley's deer are so used to visitors that they sometimes graze within a few yards of trails, but they remain wild animals capable of kicking.

animals.whereToLook: El Capitan and Middle Cathedral cliff faces
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, select rock-climbing routes on cliffs such as El Capitan and Middle Cathedral close annually, typically March through July, to protect nesting peregrines — view nests from the valley floor with a scope rather than from a nearby route or ledge.
animals.didYouKnow: Peregrine falcons can reach speeds over 200 mph in a hunting dive, making them the fastest animal on Earth.

animals.whereToLook: High alpine terrain near Tioga Pass and Mount Gibbs
animals.viewingTip: This is a critically endangered, actively managed subspecies — view only from a distance with a spotting scope and never approach a herd, especially during the fall rut.
animals.didYouKnow: Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep dropped to roughly 100 animals in the 1990s before an intensive recovery program brought the population back into the high hundreds.

animals.whereToLook: Granite boulders at Olmsted Point and Tuolumne Meadows
animals.viewingTip: Marmots at popular overlooks are used to people but should never be fed — human food disrupts their natural fat reserves needed for winter hibernation.
animals.didYouKnow: Yellow-bellied marmots can lose up to a third of their body weight during hibernation, which lasts more than half the year at high elevation.

animals.whereToLook: Valley meadows at first and last light
animals.viewingTip: Watch from a distance and never feed a coyote — Yosemite coyotes that become food-habituated around picnic areas and parking lots often have to be removed for public safety.
animals.didYouKnow: Coyotes in the valley have learned to hunt rodents in tall meadow grass using a distinctive high pounce.

animals.whereToLook: High-elevation meadow edges such as Crane Flat and Peregoy Meadow
animals.viewingTip: View from the meadow's edge with binoculars or a scope at dusk and never walk out into the meadow itself — this is a genetically distinct, state-endangered California population, and disturbing hunting or nesting habitat directly harms their already small numbers.
animals.didYouKnow: Great gray owls can hear rodents moving under two feet of snow and punch through the crust feet-first to catch them.

animals.whereToLook: High country forests and talus slopes
animals.viewingTip: Sightings are rare — if you encounter one, do not run or approach; make yourself look large, back away slowly, and give it an open path to leave.
animals.didYouKnow: A single mountain lion's home range in the Sierra can exceed 100 square miles, which is why encounters remain uncommon despite a healthy population.

animals.viewingTip: Enjoy their bold personality from a normal conversational distance, but never feed them — human food at campsites and picnic areas is both illegal in the park and unhealthy for the birds.
animals.didYouKnow: Steller's jays can mimic the calls of red-tailed hawks, sometimes to scare other birds away from a food source.
